title: MB9-09082
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Principal Appellant (XXXX XXXX XXXX), his wife, the Associate Appellant (XXXX XXXX XXXX) and their children, the minor Appellants (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX) are all citizens of Nigeria. The Principal Appellant is the designated representative of the minor Appellants.

The Principal Appellant alleges that he and his family cannot return to Nigeria because his father is a member of two cults/secret societies, the XXXX XXXX group and the XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Principal Appellant affirms that his father did not accept his refusal to join the societies and take on his role in the cults and so in 2017 began to harass, threaten and attack his family with the help of other members of his cults/secret societies. The Principal Appellant alleges that if he joined these groups he would be forced to scarify his son and his daughters would be subjected to female genital mutilation (FGM). On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the Appellants left Nigeria for the United States. On XXXX XXXX, 2018, the Appellants entered Canada and claimed asylum.
The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) determined that the Appellants' allegations lacked credibility and rejected all claims.

The Appellants assert that the RPD made numerous errors in its assessment of their credibility, in its assessment of the objective documentation, in failing to assess their children's claims independently and in failing to give weight to their supporting documentation.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 DECISION

I dismiss the appeal. Though the RPD did make certain errors, its finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection was correct. NEW EVIDENCE The evidence presented by the Appellants is rejected

The Appellants wish to introduce one new piece of evidence, namely, a letter from a physician in XXXX indicating that the Principal Appellant's sister was circumcised. The Principal Appellant, in an affidavit, explains that this evidence was not available before because it was difficult for him to convince his sister to go through a medical examination of this nature, but that when he received his rejection letter, he asked her to do this as she knows his story is true and wanted to help him. The Principal Appellant asserts that this evidence shows that circumcision of female children has been a practice in his family for a long time and that his claim is genuine.2

In order for new evidence to be admitted it must meet the criteria in section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). This means only evidence that arose after the rejection of the claim, that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection may be admitted. In the present case, the claim was rejected on March 26, 2019. Any new evidence must also meet the tests for newness, credibility and relevance set out in the cases of Singh and Raza.3

The letter from the physician is dated May 8, 2019, and thus post-dates the rejection of the claim. However, evidence of this nature could have been obtained prior to the rejection of the claim. The Principal Appellant's explanation indicates that he was unable to obtain it earlier because it was only once the claim was rejected that his sister was sufficiently motivated to help him. This does suggest that he may have been unable to obtain the evidence earlier, therefore the test in section 110(4) of IRPA is met. However, the jurisprudential test of relevance is not met. The fact that the Principal Appellant's family has a tradition of circumcising female children is not at issue.

In their memorandum the Appellants assert: "the determinative issue has been identified as being credibility and the medical report proves that FGM is practiced in the principal claimant's family and that the minor claimants' claims should have been assessed by the board member."4 I do not accept this argument. The fact that the Principal Appellant's sister was circumcised does not support the notion that the Principal Appellant's two daughters are in danger of being circumcised, given that their parents are against this practice. The risk allegations in this case, for all the Appellants, involves the Principal Appellant's father's membership in two cults and the nature of his power and influence over the activities of the Appellants, not whether FGM was commonly practiced in the Principal Appellant's family. I therefore find the new evidence is not relevant and decline to admit it.

On page 3 of the Appellants' record, they request that I hold an oral hearing without explaining why. As I have not admitted any new evidence, I may not hold an oral hearing pursuant to section 110(6) of IRPA.

The RPD found several omissions and inconsistencies between the Basis of Claim form (BOC) narrative, the amended narrative and the Appellants' testimony. The RPD also found that the objective evidence did not support the Appellants' allegations.

The Appellants submit that the RPD misunderstood the identity of one of the agents of persecution, the RPD failed to properly assess their credibility, the RPD did not give sufficient weight to their supporting documents and the RPD failed to assess their children's claims.

I have attentively listened to the recording of the RPD hearing, and have carefully reviewed the entire record. Though I have found the RPD did make some errors, I agree with the RPD that the Appellants' allegations are not credible and that the claim should be rejected. Identity of the agents of persecution

The Appellants assert that the RPD confused the XXXX XXXX XXXX with the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX which are two distinct groups. The Appellants submit: "While the XXXX is a group that is very open and transparent, the XXXX XXXX XXXX is one that is secret, thus explaining why the male claimant could not identify their names before being told by his father on XXXX 2017 (sic). While it is true that the XXXX enrolment process is one that is voluntary, it is not the case for the XXXX XXXX XXXX... the descent is automatic, which contradicts the argument of the RPD that the membership is mainly voluntary."5

Firstly, in the Principal Appellant's amended narrative he identifies the cults to which his father belongs as the "XXXX XXXX and the XXXX XXXX XXXX."6 When, during the hearing, the RPD asked the Principal Appellant to explain what he knew about these groups he indicated that he never dealt with them but that his father told him that scarification was the first step for males, that girls must be circumcised, and that he had no right to refuse to participate.7 When the RPD asked him what else he knew about these groups, he stated only that he knew these cults were wrong, against the bible and that he did not want to "move closer to them".8 The RPD then went on to state that it was aware of objective documentation describing the XXXX XXXX but not aware of any documentation about the XXXX XXXX XXXX and asked the Principal Appellant if he could explain the nature of this society. The Principal Appellant stated that he had no information. The RPD asked whether his father might have founded this society and the Principal Appellant replied that he did not know.9 Thus, it is unclear now on what basis the Appellants now assert in their memorandum that the society in question is the XXXX XXXX XXXX.

In terms of objective documentation, the Appellants had submitted three newspaper articles to the RPD regarding occult practices involving politicians, however, none of these discuss either the XXXX XXXX or XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Thus, there was no clear evidence from the Appellants before the RPD as to which of the two XXXX XXXX the Principal Appellant's father was a member.

In its reasons, the RPD cited a Response to Information Request (RIR) from 2012 on the XXXX XXXX which notes that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was created by XXXX in the XXXX.10 Throughout the XXXX XXXX where differences are noted between the reformed society and the secret society, these are made clear. The reference to the voluntary nature of membership in the XXXX cited by the RPD is clearly with regards to XXXX XXXX.11 The RPD did not err on this point.

The Appellants also accuse the RPD of having erred "in concluding that the lack of objective of evidence from the claimants on XXXX practices such as scarification when in the National Documentation Package for Nigeria that this information is said to not be available because of the secrecy of the Group. One would have to be a member to know such information."12 The Appellants assert that the RPD was therefore also wrong to state that the evidence of the scars of the Principal Appellant added no probative value.

I disagree with the Appellants that the RPD made an adverse finding based on the lack of a reference to scarification in the objective documentation. The RPD merely noted that the objective documentation did not support the Principal Appellant's assertion with regards to the ritual practice of scarification. The RPD's main point was that the objective documentation suggests that those most likely to be pressured into joining the secret XXXX XXXX would be those who had a history of involvement in the society as youths and those who were living in particular areas of the country (namely Egba, Egbado or Akeokuta areas of Ogun state), and as these criteria did not apply to the Principal Appellant that his assertions regarding his own experiences run contrary to the objective documentation.13 The RPD did not err in this conclusion. The RPD made two errors in its credibility analysis

I find that the Appellants are correct in their assertions regarding the following: a. The RPD was incorrect in paragraph 14 of its reasons that the Principal Appellant did not mention the groups to which his father belonged. b. The RPD was incorrect to find that the Principal Appellant contradicted himself regarding whether he participated in any of his father's ceremonies.

The RPD may have meant something other than what is indicated in paragraph 14 as elsewhere in its decision, it mentions that the Principal Appellant named the organizations to which his father belonged. It may be that the RPD was attempting to explain a question it posed to the Appellant. Having listened to the recording, however, it is not clear that such a question was asked. In any event, on the face of it, the statement in paragraph 14 is incorrect.

Similarly, in paragraph 15, the RPD appears to suggest that the Principal Appellant contradicted himself because he stated that he did not participate in any of his father's ceremonies yet he was obviously present at the ceremony during which he was marked with scars. I disagree that this is a contradiction. The Principal Appellant had testified that he was not a willing participant at the time, age 10, when he was scared by his father and his father's fellow cult members.

Despite these two errors in the RPD's analysis, I find the remainder of the credibility concerns to be justified and sufficient to find the allegations of risk not credible. Therefore, these errors are not determinative of the appeal. The remainder of the RPD's credibility analysis was correct

In terms of the Appellants' remaining arguments that the RPD's credibility analysis was flawed, they are the following: a. According to XXXX, there is a presumption that their allegations are true. They told their story in a straightforward manner and no material inconsistencies were identified. b. The RPD should not have drawn a negative inference from the fact that the amended narrative was submitted late. c. The RPD was wrong to draw a negative inference from the fact that the Principal Appellant had little knowledge of the groups to which his father belonged, "because the reaction of an individual experiencing a similar situation as the claimant, may be different and also subjective. As the claimant testified before the RPD, he did not accept the offer of the agents of harm nor was he interested in joining the occult group so therefore he was not very proactive in getting more information about the group."14

Firstly, it should be noted that the Appellants have not disputed all of the remaining credibility findings, for instance the RPD's finding that the threats against the Associate Appellant's father never occurred as these were omitted from the narrative.
Secondly, the presumption that sworn testimony is true can be rebutted where there are reasons to doubt its truthfulness - as in the present case.

In terms of the amendment to the narrative, the RPD did not make an adverse inference from the fact that the amended narrative was submitted late, it made an adverse inference due to the Principal Appellant's explanation for the additions. In his original narrative, the Principal Appellant only mentioned that his father was a member of the XXXX XXXX XXXX. However, nine days before the hearing, the Principal Appellant amended his narrative to indicate that his father was also a member of the XXXX XXXX XXXX and that his father consorted with many important people, who sought his assistance for spiritual protection and solving problems, specifically: "high profile politicians across the country, police chiefs, notable business men."15

The RPD asked the Principal Appellant why he added these facts to his narrative in February 2019, when, according to his testimony, he would have been aware of these facts since at least XXXX 2017 and in the case of the nature of the company his father kept, much earlier. The Principal Appellant explained that he was rushed when he initially completed his forms. The RPD was correct to doubt this explanation given that the Principal Appellant was unable to name any of these apparently important people who visited his father. The following questions and answers were recorded at roughly 0h48 of the recording: RPD: So, these people, you told me, politicians, police officers, businessmen - could you recognize them today? Principal Appellant: If I see them today, I can still recognize them. RPD: So, do you know, these people, you told me that you cannot name them - you cannot give their name but you can recognize them. So, what are they doing today - these people - are they still politicians, police officers, businessmen? Principal Appellant: Information... because I, I...I, we didn't move close to Daddy, we're trying to run away from him and its been long way tangled to him, really, but information we always get is that he's into big-time politicians, he's into big-time consultation with them cause his rise, he's part of the top hierarchy in the fraternity now. That they cannot do without him. RPD: This is your father, but those people that you told me that you've seen them often, you've seen them a lot at your house, with, going over and over again, coming, doing ceremonies or anything else, you told me that you could still recognize them. So, do you know - one of them - what he is doing today? Principal Appellant: Some of them are still in the system today. I wouldn't know if they are still in service presently. RPD: What do you mean by system? Principal Appellant: They are still in Nigeria today. RPD: Ya, still in Nigeria, OK, but do you know where they are? Principal Appellant: I don't know where they live. RPD: They are people from Ibadan? Principal Appellant: Those people? They keep coming. They come from various places to come and consort with my Dad. RPD: How did you know they were coming from other states? Principal Appellant: Mostly my mum told me. When I was growing in age - we keep seeing them coming. Coming from Lagos, coming from Ibadan, coming from Ushubu (ph) RPD: Were you talking with them? Principal Appellant: Not talking with them, they keep conversation with Daddy when I was him. We always hear... I'm just coming from so-and-so place now, we're driving from so-so place now. (...) We have a compound, we play around, when they drive in - we open the gate - who is that, that wants to see Daddy, we open the gate and Daddy comes to meet them. (..) we hear part of what they are talking. (...) RPD: So, today, you don't know where these people are or what they are doing in Nigeria? The people who were coming to your house. Principal Appellant: Because I have left him for a very long time now, I would not know if it was the same consistent, the set of people that we knew. Those days was when I was small.16

As can be seen from the above questions and answers, the Principal Appellant was unable to identify even one important person with whom his father had consorted and provided no explanation for how he knew that his father continued to consort with important people, other than what his mother told him, and his mother died in 2002. The Principal Appellant's answers on this subject were evasive, vague and he failed to explain why he amended his narrative to include the fact that important people visited his father. Thus, the issue which undermines the Appellants' credibility for the RPD was the nature of the amendments to the narrative - not the fact that they were added late. The RPD was correct to question the information in the amendments and find it not credible.

In terms of the Principal Appellant's lack of knowledge about the organizations to which his father belongs, I am of the opinion, like the RPD, that it is not credible that he would fail to inform himself about organizations which he felt could endanger his life and that of his family. Especially considering that he was exposed to these societies, allegedly since age 10, it is not credible that he would not have any concrete information to provide to the RPD about either society. The RPD did not err in this finding. The RPD's analysis of the Appellants supporting documentation was correct

The Appellants submit that the RPD's reasons, "were tainted by the negative credibility finding and the RPD gave no probative value to any of the evidence submitted by the claimants and did not analyze it properly."17

The RPD made note of the documentary evidence before it and the appropriate weight it should be accorded in paragraphs 25 and 29 to 34 of its reasons. It is evident that the RPD analysed each document separately and carefully.

In terms of the documents which directly supported the Appellants' allegations, they submitted three affidavits: one affidavit and a letter from a Mr.XXXX XXXX attesting to the attack on the Appellants' home on XXXX XXXX, 2017, one from the Principal Appellant's sister, Mrs. XXXX XXXX, confirming that the Principal Appellant's father was involved in occult practices and threatened the life of his son and one from his aunt, Mrs. XXXX XXXX, attesting to the fact that if the Appellants remain in Nigeria they may lose their lives due to the Principal Appellant's father's involvement in the occult. The Appellants had also submitted a very short email from the Principal Appellant's sister (Mrs. XXXX XXXX), much of which is not in English (and without a translation) stating that she saw their father again and he was still complaining about the occult issue.

The RPD determined that the evidence from Mr. XXXX could not be given much weight as it was established during questioning that he did not actually witness the attack on the Appellants' house but had provided the affidavit based on what others had told him. I agree with this assessment.

In terms of the affidavits from the Principal Appellant's sister and aunt, the RPD reasoned that as they contain the same allegations as those made by the Appellants and because the RPD had already found these not to be credible, it accorded them no weight. I do not agree with this rationale entirely. Though the outcome is the same, I would instead have reasoned that as I have not found the allegations credible, these affidavits, in and of themselves, are insufficient to counterbalance the negative credibility finding.

I also find that both affidavits are vague and lacking in detail when it comes to the Appellants' risk allegations. Neither mention the XXXX XXXX XXXX or the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX In the affidavit from the Principal Appellant's aunt, she affirms: "after his marriage, the father made another fearful move to invite him again to this occultic group with a serious threat of inflicting similar act of the late mother upon him through their verbal communication. (...) That if he remains within the confines of Nigeria, he might lose his life as evident from the verbal threats, his mother case and many others like such in our societies as considerations."18 No dates or specifics are mentioned. Similarly, in the affidavit from his sister, she affirms: "that XXXX XXXX ran up and down with his children in order to save his life, the most pathetic of the story was a serious of threat and intimidation on his life and after repeated attempts to involve him in the occultic movement, he sent members of the fraternity to him to harass and harm him so he can succumb to their wish but escaped the assault."19 Again, the Principal Appellant's sister mentions no specifics and no dates and it is difficult to surmise, what portion, if any of the contents of the affidavit, is first-hand knowledge.

The Appellants also assert that "the RPD gave no probative value to the newspapers simply because of the date it was published regardless that the NDP that the RPD itself used for the XXXX are dated from as old as 2006. The date should therefore not be an indicator of a probative value of an evidence. (...) the second article is indeed published in 2007, but should not be deemed irrelevant because numerous articles in the National Documentation Package are as old or older than 2007."20

The Appellants are mistaken. The RPD did not decline to give weight to the newspaper articles simply because of the date of publication. The RPD clearly stated that it gave the articles no weight because they do not mention the XXXX or XXXX societies and because they describe occurrences that are unconnected to the refugee claim at hand. The RPD did mention the date of publication of one of the articles but this was not the primary reason for refusing to accord the article weight.

Therefore, I find that the Appellants' documentary evidence was carefully assessed by the RPD and in my opinion, none of the documentary evidence has sufficient probative value to overcome the credibility concerns as identified by the RPD. The RPD did not fail to assess the minor Appellants' claims

The Appellants submit that the RPD failed to assess the minor claimants' risk of being subjected to FGM. Even if the RPD found parts of the claim not credible, submit the Appellants, the RPD should still have proceeded to analyse the minors' claims in relation to the portion of the evidence that was found to be credible.

I disagree that the RPD failed to assess the claim of the minor claimants. All claims hinged on the narrative of the Principal Appellant. The claim that the minor son would be subjected to scarification and the minor daughters would be subjected to FGM due to their grandfather's involvement in the occult was part and parcel of the risk allegations assessed by the RPD. The RPD specifically stated that though it accepted that the Principal Appellant's father was a member of a cult, it did not accept that the Appellants were at risk from this alleged agent of persecution. Thus, the RPD did not accept as credible that the minors faced the risks as alleged. Therefore, the RPD did not fail to assess the minors' claims and I agree with this assessment.

After my independent review of the evidence in the Appellants' case, I find the RPD did not err in its finding that the Appellants' risk allegations are not credible. I am satisfied, based on the evidence, that the Appellants would not be personally subjected to a risk of torture, a risk to their life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should they return to Nigeria. I am also not satisfied the Appellants have demonstrated that there is a serious possibility that they would be persecuted on a Convention ground if they returned to Nigeria at this time.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
